t: I heard a child was born before dawn. The family is resting now.
They say the child arrived safely. I suppose someone heard our prayers.
Word came from the house that the birth is over and both are resting.
I heard the first cry reached the street. That must have been a relief.
Someone said the child is healthy. I thanked the god before thinking about it.
They say everyone is tired and happy. That sounds true enough.
I heard another child has joined the village. We could use good news.
The birth went well, they say. I wonder who the family thanked first.
Someone heard the child crying through the wall. Nobody complained about the noise.
I heard the household was awake all night. At least the ending was good.
They say the mother asked for food as soon as the child settled.
A child was born last night. Perhaps blessings arrive looking this ordinary.
I heard the healer stayed until morning. The family owes many people thanks.
They say the child is loud and hungry. Those seem like promising signs.
The news reached me at breakfast. A new child and two exhausted parents.
I heard people prayed outside until someone brought the good news.
They say the family wants quiet today. That is easier to understand than miracles.
A neighbour told me the child is doing well. I hope the mother is too.
I heard the birth ended safely. I cannot decide whether fortune deserves thanks.
Someone said the father has not stopped smiling. I almost believe that part.
They say the child slept after keeping everyone awake. Sensible enough.
I heard the family needs bread and clean cloth more than visitors.
The child came safely, from what I heard. Maybe the prayers helped.
Word is the mother finally slept. Let us not wake her with congratulations.
I heard a baby arrived while most of us slept. The village feels different today.
They say the child has a full head of hair. Everyone repeats that detail.
The birth is over, and the house is quiet. I heard that much.
Someone told me the family prayed afterwards. Perhaps relief makes believers of us.
I heard the child arrived quickly. The healer still deserves thanks.
They say the new parents keep checking whether the child is breathing.
A new child was born, and half the village already claims some resemblance.
I heard the mother laughed when everyone began arguing over the child's name.
The family received good news before sunrise. We all received it by noon.
They say the child is small but strong. I hope both words are honest.
I heard a prayer was answered in that house. Others call it a birth.
Someone said the healer barely sat down. Divine help rarely looks so tired.
The new child is well, they say. I am content to leave it there.
I heard the house ran out of warm water before the child arrived.
They say both parents cried. Nobody agrees which one started first.
Word reached the square that another family has grown by one.
I heard the child quieted when held. Perhaps that is miracle enough.
They say the birth was ordinary. People sound grateful when they say it.
Someone told me the god was present. Someone else mentioned the healer.
The family has a healthy child and no sleep. I heard both facts together.
I heard the baby cried through breakfast. That household may never sleep again.
They say the mother is recovering well. I hope people give her time.
A child arrived safely. I heard thanks offered to heaven and everyone nearby.
The news is simple: one more child lives among us now.
That is good news. Do they need anything today?
I am glad the child arrived safely. The rest can remain uncertain.
Did the family ask for visitors, or are we inviting ourselves?
Perhaps the god helped. The healer still did the work before us.
A healthy child is enough reason to be thankful.
I hope someone has brought the family a proper meal.
Was the birth easy, or are people leaving out the difficult parts?
Good. I was afraid to ask after hearing nothing all morning.
I suppose answered prayers can sound like a child crying.
Let the parents decide what the birth meant to them.
Do they have enough cloth, food, and room for another child?
I believe the news. I am less certain about everyone's explanation.
The child will need a name before long. Have they chosen one?
Maybe the god was listening. I know the neighbours were.
That household deserves quiet more than another crowd at the door.
I am relieved. I had wondered why the house stayed closed.
Does the child resemble either parent yet, or only every newborn?
Perhaps we should thank the god by helping the family.
I will celebrate first and sort out my beliefs later.
Did anyone remember to feed the healer after all that work?
A birth can be ordinary and still matter to everyone.
I hope the mother is truly well, not merely being polite.
That almost sounds like mercy. I am not sure what else to call it.
One more mouth means the stores matter even more now.
I wondered whether the crying came from that house.
Did they pray before the birth, or only once it was over?
The safest answer is that many hands helped.
I hope people remember the mother's effort when telling this story.
Maybe good fortune is simply good work arriving at the right time.
Will they bring the child outside soon, or keep everyone waiting?
That family will have advice from every doorway by sunset.
I can offer thanks without pretending I understand why things went well.
A loud child usually means a tired house. Good for them.
Was anyone with the older children while everyone watched the door?
I am happy for them. That is plain enough.
Perhaps the god deserves thanks. The family certainly deserves help.
I hope the child lets them sleep before next winter.
People make every birth sound like a sign. This one can simply be welcome.
Did the news come from the family or from someone outside the door?
I would like to believe somebody watched over them.
The village gains a child and loses several nights of sleep.
They must be overwhelmed. We should ask before offering advice.
That account sounds honest. Nobody needs to improve it.
Maybe relief is its own kind of faith for a while.
I hope the new parents know how many people are pleased for them.
Let us not decide the child's future before learning their name.
Some good news asks nothing from us except a smile.
I am thankful, though I cannot say exactly who I am thanking.
Do you know whether they need food brought over?
I wonder whether the family agrees with everyone else's account.
Did anyone hear what name they are considering?
Perhaps we should visit tomorrow, once the house is quieter.
Was the child expected this soon, or did everyone hurry?
I keep thinking about all the people waiting outside.
Do they have room for the child where they live?
I wonder which detail will change by the next telling.
Did the healer say the mother needs anything from us?
Maybe gratitude matters even when we disagree about its direction.
Who first said the god had answered?
I expect the family wants sleep more than our questions.
Will the child be brought to the shrine, do you think?
Perhaps the mother has her own explanation for what happened.
Did anyone stay to help once the excitement ended?
I wonder whether a safe birth should feel less surprising.
The child will grow up hearing several versions of this day.
Do you think prayer changed anything, or merely helped people wait?
Someone should check whether the family has enough firewood.
I keep returning to the healer's part in the story.
Was there already a name waiting for the child?
Maybe this is how belief begins, with relief and unanswered questions.
I wonder who will bring the first proper meal.
Did the whole household stay awake, or only those nearest the room?
Perhaps we can be grateful without turning the child into proof.
Do they know how many people have already heard?
I wonder whether the father has slept at all.
The village will remember the birth longer than the family remembers sleeping.
Did anyone ask what the mother wants people to know?
Maybe the god helped by sending capable people to the room.
I wonder whether the child quiets for either parent yet.
Was it the first child in that household?
People speak of blessing. The family may simply speak of exhaustion.
Do you suppose they need another blanket?
I wonder what convinced you that the god was involved.
Perhaps the child's cry was answer enough for everyone there.
Did any of the older children meet the baby yet?
I wonder whether anyone has taken over the family's work today.
Maybe we should speak less about signs and more about supper.
Will people still call it miraculous after the excitement passes?
I wonder whether the healer has heard this version yet.
Did the family have everything ready, or must we find supplies?
Perhaps uncertainty is better than arguing over someone else's joy.
I wonder how long before everyone offers an opinion on the name.
Do you think the family wants thanks given publicly?
Maybe the birth changed their faith more than it changed ours.
I wonder who is watching the child while the parents sleep.
Was the house full, or did people wait outside?
I will bring bread tomorrow and leave the questions here.
Let us give the family time before knocking at their door.
I am glad they are well. That is enough for this morning.
We can ask about the name when everyone has slept.
I should find out whether they need wood or water.
Perhaps I will offer thanks tonight, in my own words.
The child is here. We can leave the explanations until later.
I will visit once the family is ready for company.
Let the household have some quiet before the whole village arrives.
I am going to check whether their work needs doing.
Maybe I will understand it better after meeting the child.
We should pass on good news without adding anything to it.
I will keep the family in my thoughts tonight.
There will be time for questions after the next full night's sleep.
I should ask the healer what supplies were used.
The family needs neighbours more than opinions right now.
I am pleased for them, whatever part heaven played.
Let us wait until tomorrow before passing the story farther.
I will bring something useful instead of another question.
Perhaps gratitude does not require certainty. I can manage that much.
We have kept each other long enough. The news is good.
I should finish my work and make room for tomorrow's visit.
Let the new parents tell their own story when they are ready.
I will save my doubts for a less joyful conversation.
The child has enough voices nearby without ours joining them.
I may stop by with food after the midday meal.
We can be thankful now and uncertain tomorrow.
I should tell my household before the story reaches them elsewhere.
Let us leave the god and the healer their separate thanks.
I will ask what they need instead of guessing.
Perhaps the meaning will become clearer when the excitement settles.
The village can celebrate without crowding the family's doorway.
I have heard enough to be happy for them.
We should let the mother decide when visitors are welcome.
I may pray for them later. For now, they need rest.
The birth went well. We need not improve the ending.
I will remember to thank the healer when we next meet.
Let us speak of something else before we turn joy into doctrine.
I should see whether the older children need company.
Maybe the god listened. I know the village did.
We can discuss causes another day. Today belongs to the family.
I will bring a blanket if they still need one.
The good news can stand without our agreement.
I should stop talking and let somebody useful reach the door.
Perhaps this is one uncertainty I can live with happily.
We will hear more once the household has recovered.
I am satisfied knowing the child arrived and the family is together.
Let us leave some quiet behind us when we go.
